abstract.p: A satirical epitaph on Sir John Spencer that notes his burial at St Helen’s and remarks that, though he did not spend all his wealth in life, it is now gone with him. It criticizes his reliance on faith rather than good works for salvation, ending with a pointed comparison to “the Turkes.”

lg.l: In greate St Helens here liest lies Sir John
Spencer, not spend all yett all is gone
Hee hoped to bee saved not by any good workes
But by his owne faith and so doe the Turkes.

div.head: Historical context and dating
div.p: Sir John Spencer (d. 3 March 1610) was a wealthy London merchant and lord mayor (1594–5), whose fortune, derived from trade with Spain and the Levant, made him one of the richest citizens of his age. A member of the Clothworkers’ Company, he rose to the highest civic offices but acquired a reputation among contemporaries for contentiousness and parsimony, and was the subject of circulating libels. He was buried at St Helen’s, Bishopsgate, where a monument commemorates him.
